Neonatal Daggernose sharks (Isogomphodon oxyrhynchus) emerge from their mothers at a total length of approximately 42.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 42.5 centimeters], a size that reflects the constraints of viviparous gestation in this critically endangered carcharhinid. Field surveys conducted in the shallow, turbid waters of the northern South American coast have consistently documented newborns exhibiting fully absorbed yolk sacs and functional jaws, indicating an immediate onset of independent foraging. This birth length is notably modest compared to related coastal carcharhinids of similar adult stature, likely an adaptation linked to the species' reliance on productive but spatially restricted estuarine nursery grounds. The protracted gestation period, lasting roughly one year, is typical of many requiem sharks and imposes a substantial energetic burden on gravid females, who must provision developing embryos via a yolk-sac placenta. Consequently, the age at birth of 365 days [ab = 365 days] represents a significant investment in each offspring, a life-history trait that becomes particularly consequential given the species' low fecundity at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. These biological constraints operate against a background environmental temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C] in the tropical waters the species inhabits, a thermal regime that modulates the pace of embryonic development and subsequent somatic growth rates.

As Daggernose shark pups transition from their neonatal phase into the juvenile stage, they embark on a growth trajectory that ultimately determines their maximal somatic dimensions. Extensive morphometric sampling by research teams in Brazil and Suriname has revealed that the species attains a striking ultimate total length of 160 centimeters [Li = 160 centimeters] for females, while males reach a comparatively smaller maximum size of 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in asymptotic length is a recurring pattern among elasmobranchs, often attributed to the elevated spatial and energetic demands of gestation in females. Large adult females, exceeding one and a half meters in total length, are capable of accommodating multiple pups and likely achieve higher fecundity over their reproductive lifespan. In terms of mass, a large female reaching her ultimate length carries an estimated ultimate wet weight of 9,560 grams [Wwi = 9,560 grams], a body mass supported by a diet of small schooling teleosts. Adult males, by contrast, plateau at a substantially lower ultimate wet weight of 7,580 grams [Wwi = 7,580 grams], reflecting their smaller frame and the absence of the volumetric requirements associated with pregnancy.

The onset of sexual maturation in the Daggernose shark occurs at a notably large proportion of the species' ultimate length, a pattern that underscores a life-history strategy prioritizing somatic growth before the allocation of resources toward reproductive activity. Extensive gonadal examinations from fishery-dependent catches indicate that females typically reach total length at puberty of 115 centimeters [Lp = 115 centimeters], a threshold at which ovarian follicles begin to mature and vitellogenesis becomes apparent. Males, consistent with their smaller adult dimensions, attain puberty at a total length at puberty of 103 centimeters [Lp = 103 centimeters], a size at which clasper calcification and testicular recrudescence signal functional reproductive capability. This size-based entry into maturity likely imposes a selective pressure on achieving sufficient body mass to support the energetic costs of mating, gestation, and parturition in a challenging coastal environment. The divergence of over ten centimeters between the sexes in maturation length parallels the species' overall sexual size dimorphism and is a common correlate of polygynous or promiscuous mating systems, where larger females benefit from increased fecundity and larger males may enjoy greater success in competition for receptive partners.

Reproductive output in the Daggernose shark is characterized by a strategy of low fecundity coupled with iteroparity, a combination that renders the species highly vulnerable to population depletion. Detailed dissections of gravid females captured in artisanal gillnet fisheries along the Amazon-Orinoco plume have established that each reproductive event yields between 2 and 8 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 8 pups per litter], a modest litter size typical of carcharhinids with a prolonged gestation. This infrequent reproductive schedule is compounded by the fact that females produce only one litter every two years [F_R_i = one litter every two years], effectively halving the species' maximum annual pup production relative to what a single-year cycle might achieve. The resulting maximum reproductive rate, when expressed over the species' lifespan, underscores the severe demographic constraints imposed by this life-history style. All of these reproductive parameters have been documented under ambient water temperatures typical of the species' equatorial range, approximately 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], a thermal condition that supports the metabolic demands of embryonic development and maternal provisioning over the extended gestation interval.

Longevity data for the Daggernose shark, derived from vertebral band-pair counts and tag-recapture analyses, indicate a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] under natural conditions, a relatively short duration compared to many larger, more slowly maturing carcharhinids at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. This relatively compressed lifespan, when considered alongside a gestation period of one year, means that a typical female may only participate in a limited number of reproductive cycles over her life, further exacerbating the species' intrinsic vulnerability. The maximum recorded lifespan of 4,380 days [am = 4,380 days] was estimated from a large female captured off the coast of French Guiana, where vertebral growth bands suggested an age at death consistent with senescent individuals at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. The combination of late maturity, low fecundity, and a restricted reproductive window renders the Daggernose shark exceptionally sensitive to even moderate levels of fishing pressure, a demographic reality that reinforces its status as one of the most imperiled elasmobranchs in the Atlantic.
